I absolutely loved this game in the 90's and it is still a great game.  My favorite aspect of this game is policies and espionage.  Kingdoms can be bought with gold or blood.  Someone declare war on you?  Well, wouldn't it be a shame if you already bribed their Generals and their army becomes your army.

You will have to manage economy and happiness.  If you're about to go broke, remember that you make gold with each enemy unit you kill.  Sometimes war is a necessity for survival.  Killing civilians, even rebellious ones will reduce happiness causing further rebellion. 

Egyptians are my favorite as population is power.  Establish you place of worship as soon as it is economically viable.  The more population you have, the more influence you can have with however you choose to express that.  Just remember to hit the Space Bar to pause the game during critical choices you make.  

Research can massively increase your efficiency.  I make custom games with one mining resource on the map.  Send one civilian to stand on the resource so others cannot build upon it.  Migrate my population and build towns around that resource.  Research advanced mining and profit.  

This is to Strategy games what Baldur's Gate 2 is to RPGs; instant classic.

This is an old-school rts game that is quite different from many of the new ones you play today. That said it strikes a balance between having many of the quality of life improvments that the oldest rts games didn't have, while still feeling like a classic.

For the most enjoyment I suggest you avoid the campaign setting completely and try the skirmish mode. You can be human or an alien/monster and each of these factions play a bit differen't but the goal is basically the same. Defeat your enemies.

For me, games are all about the experience. I love playing games but I'm not good at them, so I'm glad this comes with tons of options to customize the randomly generated maps. That said, the computer can be brutal on higher settings, it's as if the AI knows you are a human so it gangs up on you.

I like the design and detail of all the little units, seeing their animations and "special attacks" which is quite fun. Some civs have abilities that are a bit better than others, but that just adds to the challenge.

[h1]“Oh, monsters are scared. That's why they're monsters.”
~[i]Neil Gaiman[/i][/h1]

The original [b]Seven Kingdoms[/b] became a surprise hit and marked an important milestone for [b]Bill Stealey[/b]'s [b]Interactive Magic[/b]. After leaving [b]MicroProse[/b] in 1993 (right after it was purchased by [b]Spectrum HoloByte[/b]), [b]Mr. Stealey[/b] tried to continue with what [b]MicroProse[/b] did best. Creativity and simulation. [b]Wild Bill[/b] just wanted to keep doing that, without any need to keep other people's opinions in mind. And you know what? The company started  well enough. Every year there was at least one solid title from them. [b]IM[/b] started with [b]Software 2000[/b]'s charming [b]Civilization[/b] clone called [b]Exploration[/b], it got a lot of attention with [b]Trevor Chan[/b]'s [b]Capitalism[/b], in 1996 they gave us [b]Digital Integration[/b]'s [b]HIND[/b] (a totally underrated combat flight sim), while 1997? 1997 was a pure joy. They've dropped their own [b]iF-22[/b], they've released [b]Digital Integration[/b]'s [b]iF-16[/b], management fans got [b]Industry Giant[/b], turn-based audience got [b]Fallen Haven[/b] and two of [b]The Great Battles[/b] games (huge fan here), RTS audience got one of the most underrated games in the entire genre – [b]War, Inc.[/b] (seriously, the idea to add some sort of business model to our usual [b]Command & Conquer[/b] formula was beyond epic), etc. And yet, it was [b]Seven Kingdoms[/b] that shined the most.

I mean, let's just admit it. Even though some of the names I've mentioned above got a good press and ended up forming their own fan base, [b]IM[/b]'s titles, while being great, rarely got enough spotlight. Seriously, guys, how many of you even remember [b]War, Inc[/b]? Heck, most of the kids nowadays think that it's either session-based online shooter, or crappy f2p game. Both of which is technically correct (there was more than one game with that name), but come on! Cyberpunk epicness with stock market and unit customization? In 1997? And nobody even talked about it? It was just... sad (the game even got cheap re-release as a part of some budget compilation, in which it lost its awesome CDDA music for whatever reason). And yet, when [b]Trevor Chan[/b] presented his next game after [b]Capitalism II[/b]? People started to talk. Why? Well... that's an interesting question.

[url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/letande/recommended/450140/]Feel free to check out my review[/url] if you want some details, but long story short, [b]Mr. Chan[/b] and his team achieved the impossible. They've added some depth to our usual RTS formula, while also keeping things fast-paced and extremely addicting. Technically, there wasn't much to say about [b]Seven Kingdoms[/b]. While following [b]Sid Meier[/b]'s formula from [b]Civilization II[/b] and giving us either customizable “free play” campaign or pre-made scenarios with fixed goals, it wanted us to take control of one of the nations and lead it to victory. Sounds pretty boring even by 1997 standards, but the thing about [b]Seven Kingdoms[/b] was the fact that it was... a pure fun. Pretty different one too. And with so many [b]C&C[/b] / [b]WarCraft[/b] clones on market? It felt very refreshing and overall satisfying.

Sure, we still needed to attack both our enemies and the monsters called [b]Fryhtan[/b], but first, we needed to pay a lot of attention to our own territory. Just placing the building anywhere was a “no-no” in [b]SK[/b]. You needed to establish a smart logistics web between your own mines, towns, markets, sea ports and also your allies. Because yes, diplomacy was there and even though it didn't look much more complicated than what we had in [b]Age of Empires[/b], it actually was. While being easy to understand and use, diplomacy in [b]SK[/b] was pretty tricky, since it had a chance to make an impact on our reputation. Which was, like, the most important thing in the game. Just because every unit there had a loyalty meter and without loyalty... Let's just say that there was always a chance for your own people to turn against you. It was a simple, yet extremely satisfying formula. One of those that always make you come back for “five more minutes”.

Naturally, [b]Mr. Chan[/b] and [b]IM[/b], which desperately needed the next big thing, decided to keep the original formula, while adding some new features to it. Because yes, [b]SK II[/b] is a very cautious sequel. One of those that afraid of the experiments. In a way, you can say that it's pretty much the same exact thing with tons of minor changes and a couple of major additions. Let's leave the details for hardcore fans and focus on major stuff, shall we? Like I said, there are two big new things here. First – in addition to our usual human nations from the original game, there are also seven [b]Fryhtan[/b] species now. That's right, guys. In the sequel we can actually play as monsters. And [b]Fryhtan[/b] gameplay, while being pretty similar among each other, heavily differs from what we had with humans. Instead of all that reputation and economics, we should focus on brute force. Which has its own complications. As for the second big addition, we've got a proper campaign. While in the original [b]SK[/b] campaign was just a name given to [b]Civilization[/b]-like “free play” mode, here we've got a series of missions with certain goals, combined with [b]Dune II[/b]-like map. Which lets us choose the next territory to attack. That's... pretty much it when it's about casual players. Sure, [b]UI[/b] became even more juicy and feels surprisingly great, while there are tons of minor changes for those who care, but... Like I said, the idea was to give people “more of the same”. And you know what? It worked. [b]SK II[/b] is pretty much the same [b]SK[/b] thing, only better.

Unfortunately, [b]IM[/b] didn't last long enough for it to come out. Well, technically, it did, but... Let's just say that at the moment of 1999, they didn't do well. And even making the company to go public didn't help much. The official re-release of the first [b]SK[/b] wasn't enough, while [b]SK II[/b] didn't happen fast enough, so, even though it was [b]IM[/b] who helped the game to get into its pre-release state, it was [b]Ubisoft[/b] who ended up publishing the real deal back then. Which is really sad. Because honestly, [b]IM[/b] deserved the praise for this one. And yes, even though I rarely say good things about “more of the same” approach, [b]SK II[/b] was a pure joy. [b]Mr. Chan[/b] and his team added exactly what I wanted and even though it was hard not to notice that the game was just too afraid to make the next big step ([b]Seven Kingdoms: Conquest[/b] proved that it was the right decision, but that's a whole different story), I totally didn't mind having an improved version of the game I already loved.

Unfortunately, I can't say the same about the HD re-release. Even though [b]Mr. Chan[/b]'s company published the game all by itself now, what we have here is a shockingly lazy release. Not the most lazy one I've ever seen, sure. For example, the game was somewhat rebalanced, it got better hotkey support and, the best of all, there's a brand new “big map” mode, which... does exactly that – offers us much bigger scale as an option. Also, yes, the game does support 1080p resolution now. And yet, don't expect this game to be properly re-worked for modern systems. Our usual DPI bug is there, the game won't let you alt-tab properly until you'll run it in compatibility mode, etc. In other words, cheap re-release aftertaste? It's totally here. Also, the entire multiplayer was removed. Which is just ridiculous. I mean, seriously? You want people to believe it's a new and improved version of the game and yet, you give us... this? What a joke. So, as much as I love the original game, it's a thumb down from me for this exact version. Sure, there's that big map mode, but with all the “buts”? And no multiplayer? Sorry, it's a no from me. Dixi.

I have mixed feelings about Seven Kingdoms 2.  On one hand I like the expansions and updates to the roster, tech trees, and the game making spies a much more useful tool for achieving victory.  On the other hand, I'm still a bit bitter about losing access to water maps.

Though, it was probably for the best that they were removed considering how much the AI in the first game struggled to deal with them.  After all, it was pretty easy for the player to isolate themselves on an unoccupied island and then use naval technology to control the waves.  As a result the AI could only build up a force that would inevitably get crushed through multiple attacks.  Especially if you made use of siege equipment to wreak utter havoc that would take far longer to recover from then it would take you to setup for another attack.

On the other hand this game also addresses an exploit from the first game.  In the first game you could actually trap the AI to certain sections of the map by surrounding their location with markets, inns, and science towers.  Since the AI isn't allowed to attack those buildings for some reason the AI will never be able to leave the confines of your barrier.  To make matters worse/more interesting the AI will actually delete units it's tries to send past the barrier since it's default response to being unable to reach a specified location is to delete the unit that was given those orders.

On the other hand, I like this game more in some ways since you can abuse spies to take over entire enemy kingdoms with a few well placed bribes and assassinations.  This allows for the player to get away with a smaller military since you don't need to put all of your efforts into building a massive army to deal with your rivals and allows the player to put more emphasis on developing their economy.

And the game makes capturing villages easier since you don't need to get their resistance down to zero in order to capture them and allows for more rapid movement by being able to create ox carts that can take up to 10 people out of a given city at a time.  This makes it a lot easier to bus people to a new location since creating the ox carts units doesn't lower loyalty as much as recruiting 10 people out of the village would.

In conclusion the game definitely makes improvements when it comes to ground battles, but the loss of naval maps still irks me a bit to this day.
